headline: Peanut Bunker Pinned on Charles Island — Blues Crash, Bass Wait for Dark
subhead: The bait's telling the story of a Sound that's warm on top and hungry underneath, with the first bonito clock ticking toward August.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning parked off Charles Island doing more watching than fishing, and it was worth it. There's a bunker school — proper peanut size, maybe two to three inches — that's been holding tight against the rocks on the west side since the weekend, and it's not moving much even on the tide change. That's the tell. When bait balls up and refuses to run, something's pushing it from below. Sure enough, terns were working the edges all morning, and every third or fourth dive triggered a boil underneath — bluefish, mostly cocktail size but with some better fish mixed in, six and seven pounds, slashing up through the peanuts and leaving slicks of oil on the surface.

That's been the pattern across the middle Sound all week. Bunker schools are stacked from Charles Island down through the Norwalk Islands and out toward Stratford Shoal, and the blues are riding them hard during daylight. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod right now, find the birds, idle up quiet, and cast small bunker spoons or a 2-ounce Hopkins past the edge of the bait. You don't need to hit the middle of the school — the blues are working the perimeter where the peanuts get stripped off and disoriented.

Stripers are a different conversation entirely, and it comes down to temperature. Kings Point is reading right around 71 degrees, New London's a touch cooler at 69.4, and that gradient matters — the western and central Sound is holding warmer water on top, which means the bass have gone essentially nocturnal. I marked good numbers of fish on the sounder over the rockpile structure off the Norwalk Islands and along the Stratford Shoal drop-off in the afternoon, sitting deep, 25 to 35 feet down, refusing to commit during the heat of the day. Come back after dark and it's a different fishery. I fished the flat off Middle Ground Light Thursday night on the incoming, anchored up, chunked fresh bunker on fish-finder rigs, and picked off three fish in the 28 to 33-inch range in about two hours of soak time. Eels fished slow-drifted over the same structure are producing too — if you've got the patience to work them.

Fluke have followed the same logic as the bass, just without the wait for darkness. The open, shallow flats have gone quiet — too warm, not enough moving water — and the better fish have slid into the channel edges and the deeper structure where current keeps things stirred. The break off Stratford Shoal, where it drops from around 20 feet down into the 50s and 60s, has been the most consistent producer, along with the rip that builds around Middle Ground Light on a strong tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, have out-produced bare bait rigs for me two trips running. Nothing huge — most fish in the 16 to 19-inch range with a few keepers mixed in — but steady enough to make an afternoon worthwhile if you're willing to work the deeper water instead of drifting the flats out of habit.

Porgies, for what it's worth, are about the easiest thing going right now. The reef structure around the Norwalk Islands is thick with them, and anchoring up with clam or worm on a simple high-low rig will keep a rod bent all afternoon. It's not glamorous, but it's a good way to fill a cooler while you wait for the tide to turn toward a better bass or fluke window.

One thing worth flagging — we said last week that the neap tide cycle had softened current flow through the deeper Sound channels, and that's exactly what played out. The moving water through Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk gaps has been noticeably weaker the last several days, which is part of why the fluke bite went soft on the flats and why the fish that are biting have needed structure to hold current against. That should start correcting itself. The moon's building back toward full in the first days of August, and as that current rebuilds through the narrows, I'd expect the bite to sharpen — especially at Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground rip, where a stronger tide concentrates bait instead of just letting it drift.

The other thing I'm watching closely, because it's the beat I know best, is bonito. It's not time yet — water's there, current isn't quite built up enough to pin bait the way these fish like — but the Norwalk Islands are usually the first place in my zone to show signs, typically in the first half of August once the tide really starts running again. I'll be watching the bunker schools for that telltale tightening, when peanuts start getting worked over by something faster and more violent than a bluefish. If the rebuild happens the way it should over the next week, I wouldn't be surprised to hear the first confirmed report out of the Norwalk chain by early August. Until then, work the bait, fish the structure, and save your night trips for the bass — that's where the real, consistent action is right now.
